Family Health

Ulcerative colitis: symptoms, treatment and lifelong follow-up

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ulcerative colitis is a long-term inflammatory bowel disease affecting the inner lining of the colon and rectum. Treatment can control inflammation and support long periods of wellbeing, but symptoms may return. A diagnosis needs medical assessment: bloody diarrhoea, pain or weight loss should not be attributed to food or stress alone.

What ulcerative colitis does to the bowel

Inflammation usually begins in the rectum and can extend continuously through part or all of the colon. It damages the surface lining, producing ulcers that can bleed and release mucus or pus. Inflamed bowel may empty more often and urgently; bowel noises alone do not diagnose the disease.

The condition can begin at any age, often in adolescence or young adulthood, and also affects older adults. Its extent and activity differ between people and can change over time. Remission means disease activity is controlled; feeling better does not always mean all inflammation has healed.

Symptoms and when to get help

Common symptoms include diarrhoea, blood or mucus in stools, abdominal cramps, rectal discomfort and an urgent or persistent feeling of needing to pass stool even when the bowel is empty. Night-time bowel movements, tiredness, reduced appetite, nausea, weight loss or fever can occur. Poor intake and inflammation can contribute to malnutrition and anaemia.

Arrange assessment for persistent bowel changes or suspected ulcerative colitis. Seek urgent same-day help for bloody or very severe diarrhoea, fever, a fast heartbeat, inability to pass stool or gas, or a worsening flare. Contact your existing IBD team promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

Severe abdominal pain, continuous or heavy rectal bleeding, large blood clots, vomiting blood or marked deterioration requires immediate emergency care. New eye pain or vision change also needs prompt assessment. Painful or swollen joints, skin changes and mouth ulcers can accompany bowel disease and should be reported.

Why it happens, and who may be at risk

The cause is not fully understood. Genes, altered immune responses, gut microbes and environmental factors interact; the immune system’s inflammatory activity injures the bowel. Having another immune-mediated illness may be relevant to assessment, but does not establish that you have ulcerative colitis.

Family history can increase risk, although many affected people have no affected relative. Rates differ across populations, including higher reported rates in people with Ashkenazi ancestry, but any ancestry can be affected. These patterns are not a diagnosis or anyone’s fault.

Studies of the acne medicine isotretinoin and IBD have produced differing observational results. An association in a study does not prove a medicine caused an individual’s illness. Discuss new bowel symptoms and medicine concerns with the prescriber; do not stop treatment or conclude causation on your own.

Diagnosis and tests

A clinician reviews symptoms, medicines and family history, examines you and selects tests. Stool tests look for infection, including Clostridioides difficile, and may measure faecal calprotectin as a marker of intestinal inflammation. Blood tests may assess anaemia, inflammation, hydration and nutritional status; no single blood result confirms ulcerative colitis.

Colonoscopy or, in selected circumstances, a limited sigmoidoscopy allows examination of the lining and collection of biopsies. CT, ultrasound or other imaging may be useful for specific questions or complications. An upper endoscopy is not a routine substitute for examining the colon and is selected when another diagnosis, such as Crohn’s disease, is suspected.

Antibody tests are not recommended to establish or exclude ulcerative colitis. Biopsy results, bowel distribution, infection testing and the clinical picture are considered together. Follow-up may combine symptoms, stool markers and endoscopic assessment rather than relying on symptoms alone.

Medicines: different jobs at different stages

The plan depends on disease extent, severity, previous response, other conditions and your preferences. Induction treatment settles active inflammation; maintenance treatment helps prevent relapse. Oral or rectal 5-aminosalicylates, such as mesalazine/mesalamine or sulfasalazine, are commonly used for mild-to-moderate disease. Balsalazide and olsalazine are other formulations used in some settings.

Corticosteroids can help induce remission when needed, but are not maintenance treatment. Thiopurines such as azathioprine or mercaptopurine may be selected for maintenance or combination treatment, rather than as a rapid stand-alone induction treatment. Methotrexate alone is not recommended for inducing or maintaining UC remission.

For moderate-to-severe disease, options include biologics such as infliximab, vedolizumab or ustekinumab, and other targeted treatments. Tofacitinib is an oral JAK-inhibitor small molecule, not a biologic or the first oral medicine ever used for UC. Other JAK inhibitors, S1P modulators and newer biologics may be options depending on local approval and individual suitability.

Some treatments are used alone and others in combinations; there is no rule that every medicine must be combined. Discuss benefits, infection screening, vaccination, monitoring and medicine-specific risks. Antibiotics treat selected infections or complications, not every UC flare. Do not change doses, stop prescribed treatment or start anti-diarrhoeal or pain medicines without advice.

Severe flares and hospital treatment

An acute severe flare may require hospital care for blood and stool testing, close observation, intravenous fluids, electrolyte correction and treatment of anaemia, sometimes including transfusion. Intravenous steroids, prevention of blood clots and early specialist review may be needed.

If initial treatment is insufficient, the team may consider rescue medicines or surgery promptly. Routine broad-spectrum antibiotics or intravenous nutrition solely to rest the bowel are not standard for everyone. Infection, nutritional needs and complications change the plan; severe symptoms should not be managed with supplements at home.

Surgery: what is removed and what changes

Surgery may be considered for disease not adequately controlled with medicines, unacceptable treatment effects, dysplasia or cancer, or life-threatening bleeding, perforation or toxic megacolon. It is an individual decision, sometimes an emergency, rather than an inevitable outcome for a fixed percentage of people.

Removing the colon and rectum removes the bowel tissue affected by UC. Options include an ileostomy, which drains stool through an abdominal stoma into a bag, or an ileal pouch made from small intestine and connected to the anus. Pouch surgery is often staged and is not suitable for everyone; it does not simply join the small bowel to an unchanged rectum.

Surgery can substantially improve life but has risks and long-term care needs, including possible pouch inflammation. Disease outside the bowel may persist. Limited bowel removal does not guarantee a permanent cure, and even after full removal follow-up remains important. Discuss continence, fertility, sexual wellbeing and practical stoma or pouch care before elective surgery.

Supplements and “natural” treatments

Boswellia, bromelain, curcumin, psyllium and probiotics are sometimes promoted for UC. Evidence, product quality and safety vary. They should not replace effective medical treatment or delay assessment. Small adjunctive studies of curcumin do not establish a cure or a universally effective product; concentrated supplements can interact with medicines.

Probiotic strains and combinations are not interchangeable, and benefits cannot be assumed for any shop product. They may pose particular risks in seriously ill or immunocompromised people. Psyllium or other fibre supplements can worsen bloating or be unsuitable in some situations. Check any proposed product with the IBD team, especially for children, pregnancy or significant immune suppression.

Food, fluids and nutritional support

No single diet cures UC or reliably prevents every flare. A varied, balanced eating pattern supports health; a dietitian can adapt it to symptoms and nutritional needs. Claims that a low-fat diet or extra vitamin C will reliably prolong remission are not established. Choose tolerated sources of protein, carbohydrates, fruit, vegetables and healthy fats rather than imposing broad exclusions.

During a flare, smaller meals, regular fluids and temporary changes in food texture or fibre may help symptoms. Fatty foods worsen diarrhoea for some, and lactose reduction may help if lactose intolerance is present. Long-term avoidance of fibre or dairy is not necessary for everyone. A food-and-symptom diary can guide discussion; expand the diet again as tolerated.

Weight loss, poor intake or ongoing blood loss need nutritional assessment. Iron, vitamin D, calcium or other supplementation should address individual needs; vitamin B12 monitoring is especially relevant after ileal surgery or pouch formation. Ask before taking a multivitamin or high-dose supplement. Nutrition supports treatment but does not prove bowel inflammation is controlled.

UC compared with Crohn’s disease and other colitis

Ulcerative colitis generally affects the inner lining of the rectum and colon in a continuous pattern. Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the digestive tract, in patches and deeper bowel layers. Symptoms overlap, and investigations may be needed to distinguish them; sometimes IBD remains unclassified initially.

Colitis simply means inflammation of the colon. Infection, impaired blood supply, medicines and other conditions can also cause it. UC itself is not contagious, although an infection causing similar symptoms can spread and needs its own care. Surgery can remove UC-affected colon and rectum; Crohn’s disease can recur elsewhere after surgery.

Is there a cure?

Medicines can achieve and maintain remission, but currently do not provide a permanent nonsurgical cure. This does not mean treatment cannot help or that everyone will need surgery. Removing the colon and rectum eliminates colonic UC, with important trade-offs and ongoing health needs rather than a guarantee that every symptom or extraintestinal problem disappears.

Colonoscopy and cancer surveillance

Colonoscopy helps diagnose disease, assess healing and detect precancerous changes. Biopsies are examined for inflammation and dysplasia. Preparation and sedation choices depend on the procedure and your circumstances: follow the endoscopy service’s instructions rather than a universal rule to avoid all solid food for several days.

Cancer-surveillance timing is individual. Duration, extent, accumulated inflammation, previous dysplasia, family history and primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) affect risk. Current BSG guidance starts risk assessment around eight years after bowel symptoms begin, or from diagnosis when PSC-associated colitis is present; other local guidance may differ.

There is no universal colonoscopy every two or three years for all UC. Higher-risk people need closer surveillance, while confirmed rectum-only or near-population-risk disease may follow a different plan alongside ordinary screening. Agree on your next review date, and seek care for new symptoms rather than waiting for surveillance.

Ulcerative colitis in children

Children can develop UC, but this does not mean one in ten children has IBD. Persistent diarrhoea or bleeding, pain, tiredness, weight loss, slow growth or delayed puberty needs assessment. Paediatric care monitors disease activity, nutrition, iron status, growth, bone health and development.

Treatment is tailored to age, weight, disease severity and family circumstances. Oral and rectal mesalazine can both be appropriate; rectal therapy is not excluded simply because the patient is a child. Other medicines or surgery may be needed under specialist care. Do not copy adult doses or supplement plans. School support, vaccination review and transition to adult services also matter.

Complications to monitor

Complications can include anaemia, dehydration, malnutrition, weakened bones, blood clots, severe bleeding, toxic megacolon and bowel perforation. Inflammation can affect joints, skin, eyes or the liver, including PSC; kidney problems or stones can occur in some circumstances. These are possibilities, not an inevitable list for every person.

Monitoring and timely treatment reduce risk. Bowel-wall thickening on a scan is not, by itself, a UC diagnosis. Discuss new joint, eye, skin or urinary symptoms. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, fainting or severe worsening illness requires emergency assessment, including consideration of blood clots or serious complications.

Can it be prevented?

There is no established way to guarantee prevention of UC. After diagnosis, taking agreed maintenance medicines and attending reviews can reduce relapse and detect problems. Food choices, hydration, sleep, activity and stress support can improve wellbeing, without blaming you for flares or replacing anti-inflammatory treatment.

Discuss vaccinations and medication safety with the team. Do not start smoking as a UC treatment. Avoid self-prescribed NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen unless a clinician advises them. Any flare plan should explain whom to contact, what to monitor and when to seek urgent help.

Long-term outlook and everyday life

Many people have long periods of remission and lead active lives. Others need treatment changes or surgery. Agree on goals that include inflammation control, daily function, nutrition and mental wellbeing, and review progress even when symptoms improve.

Planning toilet access, travel, school or work adjustments and discussing effects on relationships can help. Psychological support complements medical care; it does not imply the disease is imagined. Continue lifelong follow-up appropriate to your medicines, remaining bowel or pouch, cancer risk and other health needs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

2025 ACG guidance and the AGA living guideline, with AGA evidence reviewed in March 2026, separate induction from maintenance and support individualized advanced treatment.

2025 BSG surveillance guidance uses disease duration and changing risk factors rather than one interval for every patient.

2025 ESPGHAN/ECCO guidance includes oral and rectal treatments and nutritional monitoring in children.

AGA nutrition advice and complementary-therapy evidence support adequate individualized nutrition without a universal diet or supplement cure.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record bowel frequency, bleeding, pain, temperature, weight changes, medicines, food tolerance and questions for your IBD team. Notes cannot diagnose UC, measure mucosal healing, set medicine doses or determine a safe surveillance interval.

When to seek help

Get urgent same-day help for bloody or very severe diarrhoea, fever, fast heartbeat, inability to pass stool or gas, or a worsening flare. Severe abdominal pain, continuous or heavy bleeding, large clots, vomiting blood, sudden breathlessness, chest pain or severe deterioration needs emergency care. Do not delay assessment or replace prescribed care with diet or supplements.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • UC causes chronic inflammation of the colon and rectum; symptoms and healing need clinical assessment.
  • Bloody or severe diarrhoea needs urgent advice; severe pain or heavy continuous bleeding needs emergency care.
  • Induction and maintenance treatments differ, and steroids are not long-term maintenance therapy.
  • Diet and supplements cannot promise a cure; nutritional advice and treatments must fit the individual.
  • Surgery, children’s care and cancer surveillance require individualized specialist plans and ongoing follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Why does UC cause ulcers?

Inflammation damages the inner bowel lining, producing sores that may bleed or release mucus and pus. Urgency and diarrhoea can accompany this injury, but symptoms alone do not confirm UC.

What symptoms should I report?

Persistent diarrhoea, stool blood or mucus, cramps, rectal discomfort, urgency, night-time bowel movements, fatigue or weight loss warrant assessment. Severe pain or heavy ongoing bleeding needs emergency care; bloody or very severe diarrhoea needs urgent same-day advice.

What diet is best?

There is no universal cure diet. Aim for adequate, varied nutrition, adapting texture, fibre, meal size or lactose only as needed with professional advice. A low-fat diet or extra vitamin C is not proven to reliably keep everyone in remission.

Can UC be cured?

Medicines control disease and maintain remission rather than providing a permanent nonsurgical cure. Removing the colon and rectum removes colonic UC, but has trade-offs, and extraintestinal disease or pouch problems may still need care.

Are steroids a maintenance medicine?

No. They can settle a flare but are not used to maintain remission. A clinician should plan steroid reduction and a suitable maintenance strategy; do not stop or change treatment yourself.

Can I replace medicines with probiotics or herbs?

No. Evidence and safety vary by product, and no supplement is a universal substitute for UC treatment. Check proposed products, interactions and special risks with the IBD team.

Does everyone need colonoscopy every two or three years?

No. Surveillance depends on duration, extent, inflammation, PSC, family history and previous findings. Ask your team for a personal schedule and report new symptoms between tests.

Is it infectious or caused by stress?

UC is not contagious, and stress alone does not explain its cause. Immune, genetic, microbial and environmental factors interact. Some infections resemble or accompany flares, so testing may be necessary.

Can a child use rectal mesalazine?

Yes, when prescribed as part of a paediatric plan. Oral and rectal treatment may be combined; suitability and dose depend on the child. Growth, nutrition and school needs require attention alongside bowel symptoms.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
